title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, alternative/integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section distills recent, reputable findings from PubMed, JAMA Network, NIH, Frontiers, and the AASM; citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This week's theme: temper the hype on **rapamycin**, and watch the growing human data on **urolithin A** as both a supplement and a topical.

- **Rapamycin reality check.** A 2026 critical review in *Aging (Aging-US)* concluded that, despite strong animal data, there is still **no clear clinical evidence** that low-dose rapamycin or rapalogs slow aging or extend healthspan in healthy adults — larger, longer trials are needed before off-label use.
- **Rapamycin may blunt exercise gains.** The new **RAPA-EX-01** RCT (40 adults aged 65–85, once-weekly 6 mg sirolimus + home exercise for 13 weeks) found rapamycin did **not** enhance — and in sensitivity analyses may have **modestly reduced** — functional gains from exercise, while adding minor side effects. Bottom line: don't stack weekly rapamycin with a training program expecting a boost.
- **Urolithin A (oral).** A JAMA Network Open RCT (adults ~71, mostly women) found urolithin A significantly improved **muscle endurance** and lowered inflammatory markers (CRP, ceramides) vs. placebo over 2–4 months, though the 6-minute-walk primary endpoint wasn't significant. An **NIH/NIA trial (NCT06274749)** testing urolithin A on glucose metabolism in adults 55+ begins recruiting **July 28, 2026**.
- **Urolithin A (topical).** Randomized clinical studies of a **1% urolithin A cream** reported reduced wrinkle depth, better hydration, and ~14% less UVB-induced redness — a gentler, mitophagy-based alternative to **retinoids** for photoaging.

Practical framing: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and be skeptical of single-supplement "longevity" claims.

sections.body:
New 2025–2026 evidence keeps HIIT as a **time-efficient** cardio tool for women — with a clear message to **pair it with resistance work** for strength and body composition.

- **Recreationally active women.** A 2025 systematic review & meta-analysis in *Scientific Reports* found HIIT reliably improves cardiorespiratory fitness and reduces **body-fat percentage** and waist-to-hip ratio, but doesn't always move total body mass — expect recomposition more than scale weight.
- **PCOS.** A 2026 network meta-analysis (23 RCTs, ~1,192 women) ranked **HIIT best** for raising VO2max and lowering **fasting insulin** and **LDL cholesterol**, while **moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)** ranked best for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). A blended week may cover both.
- **Older women.** A 2026 RCT (*Women*) of a supervised HIIT program (3×/week) showed significant gains in **aerobic capacity, lower-limb strength, and mobility (Timed Up-and-Go)**, plus drops in body-fat and visceral-fat indices and better quality of life — with no major adverse events.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and metabolic wins; **add strength training**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's studies look at *what to add* and *how to make it easier to do correctly*.

- **Adding electrical stimulation.** A fresh RCT (*Scientific Reports*, published **July 11, 2026**) found that adding **interferential current (IFC)** to supervised pelvic-floor stability exercises produced a significant extra reduction in **weekly incontinence episodes** vs. exercises alone — though most other measures (pressure, severity, quality of life) improved similarly in both groups. A useful add-on for episode frequency, not a replacement for the exercises.
- **Postmenopausal women.** A 2026 RCT in the *Canadian Journal of Urology* tested **vaginal androgen + PFMT** vs. PFMT alone in postmenopausal SUI, part of a growing interest in combining local hormonal/tissue support with training.
- **Can't isolate the pelvic floor? Try glutes.** A randomized trial found that **unsupervised gluteal-muscle contractions** cut SUI symptoms about as much as conventional PFMT (~65% vs ~63% improvement) over 12 weeks — a helpful option for women who struggle to activate the pelvic floor on their own.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard treatment** — not a replacement for it. Two recent themes stand out for HER2-positive (often TP53/p53-altered) disease.

- **Fix vitamin D deficiency.** A 2026 retrospective interventional study (*Nutrients*) of curative-intent HER2+ patients found **correcting vitamin D deficiency** was linked to better disease-free survival (adjusted HR 0.36), while *failing* to correct it carried ~1.7× higher recurrence risk. Two 2025 RCTs also reported a **doubling of pathologic complete response (pCR)** with repletion, strongest in HER2+ and triple-negative subtypes. Note: **germline TP53 mutations** are associated with early-onset HER2+ breast cancer, so genetics matter in this group.
- **Natural supplements — mechanism vs. proof.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Oncology* translational review maps supplements (e.g., **omega-3s**, green tea, curcumin) across subtypes, flagging **bioavailability limits** and, importantly, potential **interactions** with targeted therapy. Coordinate any supplement with your oncology team before starting.
- **On the horizon (standard care).** The phase-3b **DB-Guide** trial (NCT07683754) is set to test a sequential **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)**-first strategy in first-line HER2+/HR+ metastatic disease — relevant context for the earlier mechanistic finding that HER2;p53 co-mutant tumors are especially sensitive to T-DXd's TOP1-inhibitor payload.

Important framing: much of this is **early or observational** evidence. Use integrative options as *add-ons* discussed with an oncologist — not substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I stays first-line.** The AASM's April 2026 clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy issued two conditional recommendations: CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I often delivers durable improvement without drug risks.
- **Newer medication class.** A 2026 practical clinical review highlights **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** as a better-tolerated option with less cognitive "hangover" than Z-drugs/benzodiazepines, while noting cost and limited long-term data. Z-drugs remain useful only **short-term (≤4 weeks)**.
- **Supplements, honestly.** **Melatonin** shows only **modest** benefit, mostly in adults over ~55 or mild sleep-onset trouble, and is most useful for **circadian issues** (jet lag, shift work) rather than chronic insomnia. Evidence for **magnesium** in insomnia is limited.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
